# Changing a table's shape

The six verbs work down a table. Sometimes the table is the wrong shape to
begin with: a year in four columns when you wanted a year in four rows, or the
reverse.

The target shape has a name and a paper of its own. A table is *tidy* when
each variable is a column and each observation is a row [@wickham2014tidy].
Most of what a pipeline can do, it can only do to a table in that shape.
Real tables often arrive the other way, because the shape that is easy to
type into is rarely the shape that is easy to ask questions of.

Two verbs turn a table one way and back, and the names say which. `lengthen`
makes it taller and `widen` makes it wider. Nobody could remember which of
`melt` and `cast` did what, and a verb whose direction is not in its name has
to be looked up every time. `lengthen` comes first in this part, because it is
the direction data usually needs on arrival. `widen` is the way back, for the
table a person reads rather than the table a pipeline works on.

Those two rearrange what is already there. A third changes the shape without
moving a value at all. `add_combinations` is for what is *not* there: the
combination nobody recorded, the one a grouped answer leaves out rather than
reports as nothing. It closes this part because it is the case the first two
cannot reach. No amount of turning a table one way or the other produces a row
that was never in it.

One law holds the part together: **the same facts, either shape**. Reshaping
moves values, and it never invents or discards one. Where a verb has to
decide something you did not say, it prints the assumption back beside the
answer, so the choice is said aloud rather than exercised in private.
[The laws](../chapters/design-laws.qmd) show the note arriving. A reader
arriving from tidyr will recognize the job here and not the argument list,
and the appendix on [the verb you know](../appendices/d-the-verb-you-know.qmd)
holds the name-for-name map.
